newsitem.title: USA: U.S. budget deal to raise airline tax by $3 billion.
newsitem.headline: U.S. budget deal to raise airline tax by $3 billion.

text.p: Airline passengers would be tapped for an additional $3 billion in taxes over five years under the tentative budget deal struck by Congress and the White House.

By lowering an existing ticket tax and imposing a new passenger tax and international arrival and departure fees, total taxes would be boosted to $33 billion from $30 billion through the year 2002, congressional aides and airline industry sources said.

The plan calls for the current 10 percent tax on tickets to gradually be reduced, to be offset by a new tax on each segment of domestic flights and by a $24 round-trip tax on international flights, the sources said.

Low-fare airlines that rely on short hauls such as Southwest Airlines Co., said the plan unfairly shifts the tax burden to them, while the big carriers that rely on longer hauls said the plan is a step toward a more equitable scheme of basing taxes on the use of the air system.

The tax on each flight segment "will be expensive to administer and it will keep out some new entrants, which the industry needs to stay vital," said Steve Lewins, an airline analyst with Gruntal & Co.

"We are very disappointed that the Big Seven airlines have apparently convinced the House-Senate conference committee to recommend new tax measures designed by the Big Seven airlines to suppress low-fare competition," the chief executives of 18 low-fare carriers said in a joint statement.

"Any time the low-fare carriers are affected like this, obviously the consumer is the most affected," Ginger Hardage, a spokeswoman for Dallas-based Southwest Airlines said, adding that Southwest passengers will pay $45 million to $50 million the first year, rising to $135 million in 2002.

"We think it is a very good plan for domestic passengers. This is an important first step toward basing tax on use of the air system instead of on the price of the ticket," Dennis Mollura, a spokesman for Minneapolis-based Northwest Airlines Corp., said.
"When you get on the New Jersey Turnpike, you don't pay a toll based on the price of your car, you pay based on your use of the turnpike," Mollura said.
But smaller carriers are not the only ones that will be hurt by the proposed budget deal, analysts said. Major airlines that have large international operations also will see higher costs.
"It's a little bit better than the (original) proposals, but it's still going to cost everyone more money," said Jeff Long, an airline analyst with J.P. Morgan.
"It's going to hurt, primarily, those carriers with international operations, since it effectively quadruples the international taxes," Long said.

Long estimates AMR Corp.'s American Airlines will see $100 million in additional costs in the first year, while UAL Corp.'s United Airlines will face $75 million in new costs. Continental Airlines Inc.'s costs will increase about $25 million, Long said.
Travel agents came out against the higher taxes.

"We are still opposed to this kind of chicanery. Congress obviously views the travel segment of our economy and the travelling public as something that they can tax without any repercussions and that's simply not the case," Steve Loucks, spokeman for the American Society of Travel Agents, said.

Airlines will be not be able to pass the entire cost of the tax on to consumers, analysts said. Air fare battles and tough domestic competition will make it difficult to raise leisure ticket prices substantially, analysts said. Business fares will be more susceptible to increases.

Under the deal, starting Oct. 1 the current 10 percent airline excise tax would drop to 9 percent, but there would be a new $1 per passenger fee on each segment of domestic flights. That means the more connections, the more fees.
Starting Oct. 1, 1998, the excise fee would drop to 8 percent with a $2-per-segment fee. The following October, the excise tax would drop to 7.5 percent, and the per segment fee would rise to $2.25.

In subsequent years, the excise fee stays at 7.5 percent, but on Jan. 1, 2000, the segment fee rises to $2.50 and then by 25 cent each year to $3 by 2002. After that, congressional aides said it would be tied to the Consumers Price Index.
A $12 departure fee and $12 arrival fee would be imposed on international flights starting Oct. 1, up from the current $6 international departure fee.

AMR Corp. was up $2.56 at $104.56; UAL was up $1.375 at $78; Continental was up 12.5 cents; and Southwest Air was down 6 cents at $28, all on the New York Stock Exchange. Northwest Air was down 44 cents at $38.125 on Nasdaq.
